mcqs.question: Why does a 60-90 second batching window meaningfully increase effective courier capacity?
options: Concurrent orders always exceed courier capacity by 10x during lunch, requiring emergency staffing
The real bottleneck is total order volume relative to city population
It lets nearby orders share a single courier trip, turning what would be two trips into one without adding a single courier
Assignment latency only matters for orders placed after 6pm
mcqs.explanation: A batching window is a scheduling lever: combining two geographically close orders with overlapping ready-times into one courier trip multiplies effective capacity at city scale without hiring more couriers. It's not about raw order volume, staffing, or time-of-day.

mcqs.question: Why model order status as an explicit state machine instead of a free-text status field?
options: Databases can't store free-text strings efficiently
It removes the need for the courier app to ever read the order record
It automatically calculates the prep-time estimate for the kitchen
It lets every transition be validated, so concurrent writes from different actors can't leave the order in a nonsensical or ambiguous state
mcqs.explanation: With three actors writing to one record, enforcing valid transitions (e.g. a courier can't pick up an order that isn't ready) prevents races from producing an inconsistent state that support has to untangle manually. The other options aren't real benefits of a state machine.

mcqs.question: Under what condition does batching two orders onto one courier trip actually pay off?
options: Batching always improves delivery speed for every order, regardless of distance between them
Batching removes the need for an assignment engine entirely
When the orders' locations and ready-times overlap closely enough that one route barely lengthens to cover both
Only when both orders come from the exact same restaurant
mcqs.explanation: Batching helps precisely when two orders are close enough in space and time that combining them costs little extra route distance — force it on distant or mistimed orders and you add delay to both without gaining efficiency. It doesn't require a shared restaurant, and it doesn't remove the need for an assignment engine.

mcqs.question: During a lunch-hour spike, what is the actual bottleneck that stalls order flow, and what kind of fix addresses it?
options: The courier location index falls behind under high ping volume, requiring more index capacity
The database can't write new orders fast enough, requiring vertical scaling
The customer app's polling interval is too short, requiring rate limiting
The restaurant's kitchen acknowledges orders slower than they arrive, which needs a product-level fix like order throttling, not just backend tuning
mcqs.explanation: The platform's infrastructure can typically accept orders fine — the real lag is a human/kitchen bottleneck at the restaurant that blocks every downstream step. That calls for a product fix (letting a slammed restaurant throttle incoming orders, faster accept UX), not backend scaling.

mcqs.question: Why does pushing order-status updates scale better than having every client poll for status?
options: Polling is fine since restaurants only place a few orders per day
Pushing updates the moment they happen scales with actual state changes, instead of a fixed interval multiplied by every client watching every order
Polling should be replaced by requiring couriers to phone the restaurant directly
The order state machine already prevents any staleness, so neither approach matters
mcqs.explanation: Polling generates read load proportional to (clients) x (polling frequency) regardless of whether anything changed, and still leaves status stale between polls. Pushing ties load to actual state transitions, which are far less frequent. The state machine governs valid transitions, not how updates are delivered.
